article_title: Report of three experiments in the use of television in instruction, 1958–59
citation: Cincinnati Public Schools; Holmes, Presley D., Jr. (1959). Report of Three Experiments in the Use of Television in Instruction, 1958-59; Television Research in the Teaching-Learning Process. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Holmes's classification system for organizing television research on the teaching-learning process
description: Holmes developed a classification system for television research information relating to the teaching-learning process. Research information was organized and coded so that it "would be readily and meaningfully available," to identify what is now known and what is not known, thus permitting suggestions for future research. The system is the thesis's organizing artifact and the basis for its trend findings.
requirements: Research information must be organized and coded according to the classification system
target_learning_goals: organizing and synthesizing research on television in the teaching-learning process
examples: The thesis coded research information from television studies to identify what is known and unknown and suggest future research.
key_sources: Cincinnati Public Schools; Holmes, Presley D., Jr. (1959). Report of Three Experiments in the Use of Television in Instruction, 1958-59; Television Research in the Teaching-Learning Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713451

article_title: Television in army training: Evaluation of television in army basic training
citation: Kanner, Joseph H.; Runyon, Richard P.; and Desiderato, Otello. (1955). Television in Army Training: Evaluation of Television in Army Basic Training. Technical Report No. 14, Human Resources Research Office, The George Washington University, Washington 7, D. C.
title: Mass-medium television instruction can replace regular instruction with no loss in learning effectiveness
description: The report draws an applied design conclusion from its experimental comparisons: instruction of the types studied could be delivered by television as a mass medium without sacrificing learning. It states the results "suggest that, should conditions require the Army to adopt a mass medium of instruction such as television", the instruction types used in the study could be presented "with the strong assurance that there would be no loss in learning effectiveness". The principle is grounded in the study's comparisons of television, kinescope, and regular instruction with the same instructors.
requirements: Instruction prepared for television and delivered by the same instructors who give regular instruction, as in the study's procedure
constraints: Applies to the Army basic training subject matter and instruction types used in this study
target_learners: Army basic trainees, including low- and high-aptitude groups
target_learning_goals: Achievement of basic training subject-matter objectives, measured immediately and after one month
examples: The evaluation compared television and regular instruction for 14 selected hours of basic training, with achievement tests administered immediately and after one month.
key_sources: Kanner, Joseph H.; Runyon, Richard P.; and Desiderato, Otello. (1955). Television in Army Training: Evaluation of Television in Army Basic Training. Technical Report No. 14, Human Resources Research Office, The George Washington University, Washington 7, D. C. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02719927

article_title: Shooting live television shows on film
citation: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Limit television instruction to small viewing groups, bounded daily totals, and short continuous viewing periods
description: The summarized army TV research sets concrete operating limits for instructional television: group size, daily curriculum time, and continuous viewing time are each capped. The abstract states "Not more than 20 students should view one TV screen" and that "no more than 30 minutes of continuous viewing should be attempted", with a four-hour daily curriculum ceiling. These limits function as design parameters for classroom TV use.
requirements: A TV receiver screen adequate for the group size; the abstract separately sets a 16-inch minimum screen for 20 viewers.
constraints: Limits are stated for army training contexts with the receiver technology of the period; the abstract prints no test statistics supporting the thresholds.
target_learners: Army trainees in classroom television instruction
target_learning_goals: Delivery of curriculum content via television without overloading viewers
examples: The abstract's conclusions specify caps of 20 students per screen, four hours of total curriculum per day, and 30 minutes of continuous viewing.
key_sources: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners
citation: Didem Koban Koç & Serdar Engin Koç. (2017). On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 93–110. https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1275
title: TV-series video-clip treatment for teaching formulaic sequences (Homeland and Shades of Blue clips)
description: An instructional element consisting of short clips from two American drama TV series, Homeland and Shades of Blue, each containing one target formulaic sequence. The article states: "In each week, the participants were exposed to 10 clips from the TV series. Each of the clips had one FS," with each clip lasting an average of 10 seconds. FSs were preselected from episodes and frequency-checked against the British National Corpus and the Corpus of Contemporary American English, yielding 55 FSs of which 30 unknown targets were retained after pretesting. Clips were screened to avoid violent or obscene content.
requirements: Clips must be shown long enough for learners to understand the context in which each FS is used
A weekly list of the 10 FSs is provided to learners
Instructor provides the FS definition after each clip
constraints: Clips came from scripted drama speech, which the authors note tends to be artificial and inauthentic compared with naturally occurring speech
target_learners: first-year advanced EFL learners in an English Language Teaching program
target_learning_goals: learning and retention of 30 target formulaic sequences
examples: The experimental group watched the clips with explicit instruction while the control group received the same explicit instruction and pair-work scenario creation without video
key_sources: Didem Koban Koç & Serdar Engin Koç. (2017). On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 93–110. https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1275
